summary: For learners aged 10-11, this guidance builds the bridge from arithmetic representation fluency to algebra. Three connected objectives: (1) translate a word problem into BOTH a bar model with a labelled unknown AND an algebraic equation (e.g. 4x + 27 = 87, where x = 15), mapping each symbol to each part of the bar; (2) read the equals sign RELATIONALLY — the two sides name the same amount, so you may do the same operation to both — rather than as 'work out the left-hand side'; (3) explain why a pie chart, a fraction and a percentage that show the same portion of the same whole all represent one proportion. A supporting objective is plotting ordered pairs from a table onto a coordinate grid and stating what each axis and point MEANS in the situation before reading the relationship. The relational equals sign is the load-bearing idea: research on children's understanding of equality (e.g. Falkner, Levi & Carpenter) reports that many learners read '=' as 'do the calculation'; that reading gives no reason for subtracting 27 from both sides, so learners who hold it may fall back on memorised rules that they can misapply.
misconceptions: Reads '=' in an equation as 'work out the left-hand side' (operational), so cannot justify doing the same operation to both sides
Treats a bar model and an algebraic equation as unrelated — can draw one but not see it as the other's structure
Treats a pie chart, fraction and percentage as different things rather than one proportion of the whole
Reverses coordinates or reads a point's value without connecting it to the quantity the axis represents

activities.title: Build the bar, build the equation, balance it
steps: Take the word problem: 'I think of a number, multiply by 4, add 27, and get 87.'
Draw a bar model: four equal unknown parts plus a 27-block, all equal in length to an 87-bar.
Write the matching equation 4x + 27 = 87 beneath, and point to where the x, the +27 and the 87 each appear in the bar.

Treat the equation as a balance with two equal sides. Try removing 27 from only one side and say what would go wrong; then remove 27 from BOTH sides (leaving 4x = 60) and explain why the two sides stay equal.
State in your own words why '=' lets you do the same thing to both sides, and finish solving (4x = 60, so x = 15).

If a dynamic model is available, size an unknown bar and watch the equation assemble; in a balance-beam mode, removing weight (such as the 27) from only one pan tips the beam, so removing it from both becomes a felt necessity, and the 27 vanishing on both sides at once mirrors the equation step.
activities.insight: A bar model and an algebraic equation are the same structure in two forms; the equals sign is a promise that both sides are the same amount, which is exactly why you may apply the same operation to both sides.

activities.title: Argue a classmate out of the operational equals sign
steps: Respond to a partner (real or role-played) who claims: '= just means work out 4x + 27, and the answer is 87.'
Explain why that reading breaks down when you need to solve for x, using the balance idea that both sides name the same amount.

Respond to the same partner, who points to a pie slice that is 40% of the whole and claims '40% is a different thing from that pie slice' — argue why the slice, the fraction 2/5 (40/100) and 40% of the same whole are one proportion.
Keep the exchange as justification, not a scored answer: push every assertion to a reason.
activities.insight: Relational equality and proportion equivalence become more convincing when you have to defend them against a plausible wrong view, not just assert them.

activities.title: One proportion, three pictures
steps: Look at a pie chart with one quarter shaded.
State the fraction (1/4) and the percentage (25%) it represents.
Explain whether these are the same amount or three different things, pointing to the same whole in each form.
Repeat with another proportion of your choice, converting among pie chart, fraction and percentage and justifying the shared magnitude.
If a linked display is available, change one form (e.g. drag the pie slice) and watch the fraction and percentage update together.
activities.insight: A pie chart, a fraction and a percentage are different representations of one proportion of the same whole, not three separate quantities.

activities.title: Plot the table and say what the points mean
steps: Take a small table of paired values and plot each pair as an ordered point on a coordinate grid.
Before reading any relationship, name what the horizontal axis means and what the vertical axis means in the situation.
For one point, say what its two coordinates MEAN (e.g. 'at 3 hours the cost is £12'), not just the numbers.
Describe the relationship you see between the quantities, in words tied to the situation.
Check for reversed coordinates by asking whether the point lands where that situation should put it.
activities.insight: A coordinate point carries situational meaning: naming what each axis and coordinate represents is what turns plotted dots into an interpretable relationship.

checkQuestion: A classmate is solving 4x + 27 = 87. They say: 'The equals sign means work out 4x + 27, and the answer is 87.' First: do you agree that's what the equals sign is telling us here? Then take this problem — 'I think of a number, multiply it by 4, add 27, and get 87' — show it as a bar model AND as an equation, and explain why you're allowed to subtract 27 from both sides.
checkAnswer: No single scored answer — listen for the child rejecting the operational reading and treating '=' relationally (the two sides are the same amount), mapping the word problem to both a bar with an unknown part and 4x + 27 = 87, and justifying 'subtract 27 from both sides' by the balance idea (keeping the two sides equal) rather than by a memorised rule.
